extracted.intended_audience: professional mathematicians and advanced students (readers of a 19th-century mathematical journal)
extracted.subtask_description: Methods and formulae for computing coordinates of the centre of gravity (centroid) of lines, perimeters, polygonal surfaces, triangular plates, pyramids and general polyhedra via decomposition and weighted averages; includes related results on loci of centres for inscribed quadric surfaces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weighted-average formula for centre of gravity of composite body
rubrics_metrics.description: When a body is composed of parts whose centres of gravity and weights are known, the coordinates of the whole body are X = (w x + w' x' + ...)/(w + w' + ...), and similarly for Y and Z.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By the theory of parallel forces: X = (Σ w_i x_i)/Σ w_i, Y = (Σ w_i y_i)/Σ w_i, Z = (Σ w_i z_i)/Σ w_i. If all w_i are equal this reduces to the arithmetic mean of coordinates. Equations (A) and (B) in the text present these relations and note simplifications when weights are equal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Centre of gravity of a straight line (uniform)
rubrics_metrics.description: The centre of gravity of a uniform straight line coincides with the midpoint of its extremities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obtain by taking n = 2 in the weighted-average formula: coordinates = (x + x')/2, (y + y')/2, (z + z')/2.

rubrics_metrics.name: Centre of gravity of the perimeter of a polygon
rubrics_metrics.description: The centre of gravity of the perimeter is the weighted average of the centres of the sides, weights being the side lengths (or proportional to them).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the angular points are x y z; x' y' z' etc., coordinates of centre of first side are 1/2(x+x'), 1/2(y+y'), 1/2(z+z'); multiply these by the side's length (weight), sum for all sides and divide by total perimeter (Σ weights) to obtain the perimeter-centroid. When all sides lie in one plane the first two coordinates suffice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Centre of gravity of a triangular plate (uniform thin plate)
rubrics_metrics.description: The centre of gravity of a uniform triangular plate coincides with the centroid of its three vertices (average of vertex coordinates).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By the theorem: centroid = (x1 + x2 + x3)/3, (y1 + y2 + y3)/3, (z1 + z2 + z3)/3. This is obtained by taking n = 3 in the general weighted-average formula.

rubrics_metrics.name: Centre of gravity of a polygonal surface via triangulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Resolve the polygonal surface into triangles from a chosen reference point; the surface centroid is the weighted average of the centroids of those triangles, weights proportional to triangle areas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For angular points x y z, x' y' z', etc., form triangles from a reference vertex and remote vertices; centroid of each triangle is average of its vertex coordinates; multiply by its area (weight) and sum, dividing by total area (Σ weights). When polygon sides lie in one plane, only X and Y are needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Centre of gravity of a triangular pyramid
rubrics_metrics.description: The centroid of a homogeneous triangular pyramid coincides with the centroid of four equal weights placed at its vertices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Take n = 4 in the weighted-average formula to obtain coordinates: (x1 + x2 + x3 + x4)/4, etc. This gives the coordinates for the triangular pyramid's centre of gravity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Centre of gravity of a general polyhedron via decomposition into triangular pyramids
rubrics_metrics.description: Resolve a polyhedron into triangular pyramids by selecting a point and drawing planes through remote angular points; the polyhedron centroid is the weighted average of the pyramids' centroids with weights proportional to their volumes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If angular points are a1, a2, ... then decompose into tetrahedra; use coordinates of each pyramid's centroid (from triangular pyramid formula) and weights proportional to pyramid volumes (expressible in coordinates) to compute the polyhedron centroid via Σ(w_i x_i)/Σ w_i, etc. Equations (6) in the text give the general form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between centroid of equal weights at vertices and surface centroid
rubrics_metrics.description: The centre of gravity of a system of equal weights placed at the vertices of a polygon is generally different from the centroid of its surface, except for triangles where they coincide.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scholium: equations (2) and (4) show these are different in general; Lardner's previous remark that they coincide always is incorrect. Use explicit comparison via formulas to check equality; equality holds only for triangles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical method for forming logarithms using tables and remainders
rubrics_metrics.description: To find the logarithm of a number (or the number for a given logarithm) using logarithmic and anti-logarithmic tables by iterative lookup: refer to tables for initial figures, subtract logs, multiply remainders to set initial figures to fixed size, and continue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure illustrated in examples: take proposed number, multiply or isolate index; refer to 'Logarithmic' table and pick the log next less than the given mantissa; subtract to get a remainder; multiply remainder by suitable figure to bring next remainder to a specified number of initial figures (e.g., 100); consult next table, and continue iteratively to extract successive digits. Example: finding number whose log is 9.5410780723 is worked step-by-step multiplying remainders and extracting factors which are multiplied together to get the number.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inverse procedure: finding number from its logarithm via anti-log tables
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a logarithm (index + mantissa), determine the corresponding number by consulting anti-log tables: find the closest smaller log in table I, work with differences, find successive factors from tables II, III, etc., and multiply those factors to obtain the number.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by worked examples: reject the index, use anti-log table I to note the log next less than given; write down the difference; consult table II for log next less than the difference and subtract, obtaining a sequence of differences mapping to factors; multiply the series of factors (often powers of 10 offsets) to form the required number. A 'superfluous labour' trick shows how to avoid rewriting settled figures by tabular alignment of successive factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using logarithmic tables to specified decimal places (practical examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: To compute logs or anti-logs to a fixed number of decimal places (e.g., six places), carry out the iterative table-lookups and multiplications only as far as necessary to obtain the desired precision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples computing log(48.76) to six places and conversely obtaining the number with log 1.688064 illustrate truncating the iterative process once required digits are determined, and show intermediate multipliers and subtractions used in standard table methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion for expressing quadratic surface equation as product of two linear factors (U = V W)
rubrics_metrics.description: To test whether a second-degree surface U can be represented as the product V W of linear functions V and W, solve the quadratic (I) (in text) whose roots ai and ci correspond to linear factor coefficients, and use derived relation (4) to analyze values.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set U = V W with V and W linear; determine ai and ci as roots of the quadratic fl» — ca + a = 0 (I). Derive (4), a quadratic in z, whose nature (real/imaginary roots etc.) and consequent properties determine the type of surface. The text gives an example transforming the equation and interpreting resulting factorization to conclude the surface is hyperboloid of one sheet.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification by rectilinear intersections parallel to coordinate planes
rubrics_metrics.description: Classify surfaces of second degree by the number of planes parallel to a coordinate plane which yield rectilinear intersections: hyperboloid of one sheet — two such planes; hyperbolic paraboloid — one or none; cone — planes coincide (double root).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation: when decomposition leads to two distinct z-roots, there are two rectilinear intersections parallel to that coordinate plane; equal roots correspond to coincident planes giving a cone; imaginary/unreal roots correspond to hyperboloid of two sheets. Use isolation in x, y, or z to check presence/absence of such planes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Condition for quadratic form to be sum or difference of two squares
rubrics_metrics.description: An equation in two variables of the form Au^2 + Bv^2 + ... + 1 = 0 is resolvable into the sum or difference of two squares if certain algebraic relations among coefficients hold (as derived in equations (1), (2), (2') ).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derive relationships such as 4BXI— iP)(1-iw»)=B«(n-i^f/i)» and set parameters so that (1) reduces to a sum or difference of squares. Use substitutions tn = a + a^-1, n = β + β^-1 and trigonometric parametrizations a + a^-1 = 2 cos θ to recast into forms (2') involving cosines, aiding classification between sum and difference cases and allowing restrictions on reality of coefficients.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equation of surfaces of second order touching three given planes
rubrics_metrics.description: Surfaces of second order tangent to the three given planes u = 0, v = 0, w = 0 have a general equation of the form (4) (or the trigonometric variant (6)/(6')), involving parameters A, B, C and combinations ensuring tangency and classification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assume general quadratic with squared-coefficients for convenience: AV + BV + Cw + AB(... )uv + AC(... )uw + BC(... )vw + linear terms + 1 = 0. By substituting u = 0 etc., require the resulting plane-section equations be sum/difference of squares leading to conditions on coefficients (expressions for /, m, n, q, r). If A,B,C are real in certain ways the surface is hyperboloid of one sheet/hyperbolic paraboloid; cones/cylinders appear as limiting cases (A,B,C large) and are included. Use symmetry in parameters for compact form; see (6) and (6').

rubrics_metrics.name: Equation of surfaces of second order touching four planes (inscribed in tetrahedron)
rubrics_metrics.description: Surfaces tangent to four given planes (faces of a tetrahedron) can be expressed in form (9) or (10)/(10') with parameters constrained (e.g., a β γ = 1 or sum conditions) obtained by requiring plane-sections to be sum/difference of squares.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start from general quartic (9), set each variable = 0 in turn, use prior two- and three-plane conditions to solve for parameter combinations (/, m, n, q, r, s) and reject extraneous roots that would reduce the equation to lines/planes. The resulting symmetric forms (10)/(10') include trigonometrically-parameterized coefficients and carry conditions such as aβγ = 1 or angular sum = 2π for reality and classification. The derivation shows which parameter choices correspond to hyperboloids, paraboloids, cones, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equation of surfaces touching faces of a parallelepiped and locus of centres
rubrics_metrics.description: For a parallelepiped (faces given by u − a = 0 etc.), the equations of second-order surfaces tangent to its faces can be obtained by appropriate substitution into (6) and solving for A, B, C; the centres of all such inscribed quadrics coincide at the intersection of the diagonals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Substitute shifted coordinates (u − a, v − b, w − c) into general three-plane-touching form, expand and equate coefficients to solve for A, B, C; eliminate them to get condition (14) or trigonometric variant (14'). The centre of every such surface is fixed at the intersection point of the parallelepiped diagonals (origin chosen at diagonal intersection). Remarks: if corresponding faces of two parallelepipeds are parallel, generally no quadric touches all eight unless their diagonal intersections coincide.

rubrics_metrics.name: Locus of centres of second-order surfaces inscribed in a parallelopiped
rubrics_metrics.description: The locus of centres of quadrics tangent to the faces of a given parallelepiped degenerates into a single point — the intersection of the diagonals of the parallelepiped.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: if a quadric touches two parallel planes, the line joining contact points is bisected at the centre; applying to three pairs of parallel faces forces centre to lie in three perpendicular mid-planes, whose intersection is the diagonal intersection point; hence centre is unique.
